Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- London commuters crammed onto buses, scrambled for taxis, cycled or simply walked on Wednesday as a strike by Tube workers shut down most of the subway network. Commuters queue for packed buses in London on Wednesday morning. The strike began Tuesday at 7 p.m. (2 p.m. ET) but the first full effects were felt during Wednesday's morning commute. The strike was set to last for 48 hours with a normal service resuming Friday morning, according to Transport for London (TfL), which runs the city's transportation network. The RMT trade union called the strike after talks with management over pay, job cuts, and disciplinary issues broke down. "RMT doesn't resort to industrial action lightly," General Secretary Bob Crow said in a statement. "The fact is that Tube workers have been driven into walking out today." Transport Commissioner Peter Hardy said the talks had been making progress on all issues and he urged the RMT to return to the table. "The RMT leadership says we were close to a deal," Hardy said in a statement. "If that is the case, then they should call off the strike, return to talks ... and resolve this issue without any more disruption to Londoners." TfL was running extra buses and free shuttle services across the River Thames during the strike. Electronic travel cards used for the TfL network were temporarily being allowed on all train lines in greater London, it said. While most services on the Tube were shut because of the strike, one line -- the Northern line -- was running normally and five others were running on a reduced schedule, TfL said. "It's been really good," a girl on Oxford Street told CNN about her commute. "The Northern line is running perfectly." Still, some bus services were packed with commuters who normally ride the underground trains or who failed to find a taxi. "I think we'd all like to strike for more money, but unfortunately we can't," said one woman at Oxford Circus, where the Tube is closed. Others hit the pavement and walked. "It's OK -- quite refreshing," said a man on Regent Street. He said he had just walked from Liverpool Street Station, a train station as well as a Tube stop that is more than 2.5 miles away. The RMT represents about half of the 20,000 employees on the Tube, a TfL spokeswoman said. Other unions including Unite and TSSA represent the rest, she said, and were not on strike.

LONDON, England (CNN) — London commuters crammed onto buses, scrambled for taxis, cycled, or simply walked on Wednesday as a strike by Tube workers brought most of the subway network to a standstill.

Commuters queued for packed buses across London on Wednesday morning. The strike began Tuesday at 7 p.m. (2 p.m. ET), but its first full effects were felt during Wednesday’s morning rush hour. According to Transport for London (TfL), which runs the city’s transportation network, the strike was set to last 48 hours, with normal service expected to resume Friday morning.

The RMT trade union called the strike after talks with management over pay, job cuts, and disciplinary issues broke down.

“RMT doesn’t resort to industrial action lightly,” General Secretary Bob Crow said in a statement. “The fact is that Tube workers have been driven into walking out today.”

Transport Commissioner Peter Hardy said the talks had been making progress on all issues and urged the RMT to return to the negotiating table.

“The RMT leadership says we were close to a deal,” Hardy said in a statement. “If that is the case, then they should call off the strike, return to talks ... and resolve this issue without any more disruption to Londoners.”

During the strike, TfL was running extra buses and free shuttle services across the River Thames. It also said that electronic travel cards used on the TfL network were being temporarily accepted on all train lines in Greater London.

While most Tube services were suspended because of the strike, one line — the Northern line — was operating normally, and five others were running on a reduced schedule, TfL said.

“It’s been really good,” a girl on Oxford Street told CNN of her commute. “The Northern line is running perfectly.”

Still, some bus services were packed with commuters who normally take the Underground or who had been unable to find a taxi.

“I think we’d all like to strike for more money, but unfortunately we can’t,” said one woman at Oxford Circus, where the Tube station was closed.

Others took to the pavement and walked.

“It’s OK — quite refreshing,” said a man on Regent Street. He said he had just walked from Liverpool Street Station, a rail station and Tube stop more than 2.5 miles away.

The RMT represents about half of the Tube’s 20,000 employees, a TfL spokeswoman said. Other unions, including Unite and TSSA, represent the rest and were not on strike, she added.

## Breaking News: London Tube Strike Causes Major Disruption Across Capital

**London** — A strike by London Underground workers has brought widespread disruption to the capital’s transport network today, leaving commuters facing long delays, crowded buses and packed rail services during the morning rush hour.

Transport for London said several Tube lines were either suspended or running severely reduced services, with disruption expected to continue throughout the day and into the evening.

### Affected Tube Services

According to the latest update from TfL:

- **Central line**: Severe delays, with limited trains operating.
- **District line**: Part suspended, with reduced service on remaining sections.
- **Piccadilly line**: No service across much of the route.
- **Victoria line**: Severely reduced service.
- **Jubilee line**: Limited service, with stations subject to short-notice closures.
- **Northern line**: Major disruption, with long gaps between trains.
- **Circle and Hammersmith & City lines**: Suspended for much of the morning.
- **Bakerloo line**: Reduced service.

Some stations have been closed temporarily because of overcrowding, while others are open for interchange only.

TfL has urged passengers to check before they travel and to avoid making unnecessary journeys.

### Extra Buses and Alternative Routes

To ease pressure on the network, TfL said it has deployed **additional buses on key routes**, particularly into central London and around major transport hubs including Victoria, Waterloo, King’s Cross, Liverpool Street and Stratford.

However, officials warned that buses are also expected to be significantly busier than usual, with heavy road congestion reported across central and inner London.

The **Elizabeth line**, **London Overground**, **DLR**, **National Rail services** and **tram services** are operating, though some are experiencing heavier passenger numbers due to the Tube disruption.

Cycling hire schemes have also seen increased demand, with some docking stations in central areas running low on available bikes.

### Oyster and Travelcard Arrangements

TfL said **Oyster cards, contactless payments and Travelcards remain valid** on services that are operating.

Passengers with Travelcards may use them on available alternative TfL services, including buses, London Overground, DLR and the Elizabeth line, within the relevant zones.

TfL also said some ticket acceptance arrangements are in place with National Rail operators, though passengers are advised to check specific routes before travelling.

Customers who are unable to complete their journeys may be eligible to claim a refund, depending on the circumstances.

### Commuters React

Many commuters described the morning journey as “chaotic” and “frustrating.”

“I left home an hour earlier and I’m still late,” said Priya Shah, a finance worker trying to reach Canary Wharf. “The buses are packed, the roads are barely moving, and everyone is just checking their phones trying to find another route.”

At King’s Cross, commuter Daniel Hughes said he had abandoned his journey after multiple failed attempts to board alternative services.

“You expect disruption during a strike, but it feels like there’s no real backup,” he said. “Every option is overloaded.”

Others said they supported the workers’ right to strike but wanted a faster resolution.

“I understand why people strike, especially with pay and conditions the way they are,” said Maria Collins, a teacher from west London. “But ordinary workers get caught in the middle.”

### Union and TfL Response

Union leaders said the strike is part of an ongoing dispute over pay, staffing levels and working conditions. They accused transport bosses of failing to offer meaningful guarantees on job security and shift patterns.

TfL said it remains open to talks and urged unions to return to negotiations.

“We apologise to Londoners for the disruption,” a TfL spokesperson said. “We are doing everything possible to keep the city moving, but customers should expect significant disruption and plan ahead.”

City officials have called on both sides to reach an agreement, warning that repeated strikes risk causing serious economic damage to businesses already facing pressure from rising costs and reduced footfall.

Further disruption is expected if the dispute is not resolved. TfL said services may start later than usual tomorrow as trains and staff return to normal schedules.

**By CNN Staff**  
**June 10, 2009**

**LONDON, England (CNN)** — Millions of commuters faced severe travel disruption Wednesday after workers on the London Underground began a 48-hour strike Tuesday evening, shutting down much of the capital’s subway network.

The walkout, which began at 7 p.m. local time Tuesday, was expected to continue until Thursday evening. Transport for London warned passengers to avoid unnecessary travel and to use buses, overground rail, river services or bicycles where possible.

London Underground said it was attempting to run limited services on some lines, but many stations were closed and large sections of the network were suspended. Long lines formed at bus stops Wednesday morning, while major roads into central London were heavily congested.

The strike was called by the National Union of Rail, Maritime and Transport Workers, known as the RMT, and backed by members of the Transport Salaried Staffs’ Association, or TSSA. The unions said the dispute centered on pay, job security and working conditions, including concerns over proposed staffing reductions and disciplinary issues involving union members.

RMT General Secretary Bob Crow accused London Underground management of refusing to provide adequate guarantees over jobs and conditions.

“Our members are not prepared to accept threats to their livelihoods or a pay offer that fails to recognize the pressure they are under,” Crow said in a statement. “This strike could have been avoided if management had taken these concerns seriously.”

Mayor Boris Johnson criticized the walkout, saying it would hurt workers and businesses already under pressure during the recession.

“It is Londoners who will suffer as a result of this unnecessary strike,” Johnson said. “I urge the union leadership to get back around the table.”

The London Underground, commonly known as the Tube, carries more than 3 million passengers on a typical weekday and is one of the world’s oldest and busiest metro systems.

The RMT is one of Britain’s most prominent transport unions, representing workers across rail, maritime and public transport sectors, including train operators, station staff, maintenance crews and signal workers. It has frequently taken industrial action in disputes over pay, safety and staffing levels.

The TSSA represents clerical, technical, supervisory and managerial staff in the transport and travel industries. Its members on the Underground include administrative and salaried employees, some of whom joined the dispute in support of demands over pay and job protections.

Not all transport unions were involved in the strike, and London Underground said it hoped to operate as many services as possible using available staff. However, officials warned passengers to expect major delays and station closures throughout the 48-hour period.

Businesses in central London reported lower foot traffic Wednesday morning, while some commuters said they had walked several miles or worked from home.

“I left an hour earlier and still couldn’t get anywhere near my office,” said one commuter at Waterloo station. “The buses are packed, and no one seems to know what’s running.”

Talks between union leaders and London Underground management were expected to continue, but there was no immediate sign of a breakthrough.
